extracted.intended_audience: novelists and serious students of fiction/craft
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques for rendering a character's inner life and the novel's point of view by dramatizing moments, scenes, and surface images rather than authorial exposition. Covers when to use or dispense with a narrator, how to reveal facts indirectly, and how to apply dramatic method to undramatic subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize a character's consciousness (show surface images)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange matters so a character’s thought is made intelligible by a direct view of its surface: the immediate flaw or ripple of the moment, and the next and the next, enact the story rather than an authorial summary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Render thought as passing images crowding across the stage (e.g., Strether’s mind): show the fleeting impressions, gestures, and looks that a spectator could detect rather than penetrating hidden depths. This is drama applied to consciousness: the spectator must judge by appearances; do not substitute retrospective explanation for demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial non-intervention / refrain from telling on authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The author should accept nothing on authority for the reader—he 'most carefully refrains from using his pen'—and should avoid interposing his own vision into the narrated experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not supply the reader with the author’s private knowledge; instead construct scenes that allow the reader to observe and infer. Authorial intrusions that explain or reinterpret events for the reader will disturb the intended impression and weaken dramatization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid retrospective exposition; prefer demonstration over summary
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere account of the mind’s working, 'after the fact', is statement where we look for demonstration and therefore lacks force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid summarizing a character’s internal process after it occurs. Instead stage moments that demonstrate how the mind works in time; let sequences of impressions enact the process rather than telling it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withhold full disclosure; reveal internal developments gradually
rubrics_metrics.description: If the narrator begins to expound a character’s inner substance he is obliged to disclose it wholly at once; otherwise exposition misleads. Gradual revelation preserves deliberation, restraint, and suspense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not allow a narrator who shares privileged knowledge to hold back partial truths; instead use a method that permits piecemeal disclosure—deliberation and suspension of information can be achieved by dramatizing thought over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use repeated, incremental glimpses to show a change of mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Bring a character’s mind into view at different moments, multiplied until the silent change is apparent though no explicit statement is made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct successive small scenes or impressions that together make the evolution of feeling or purpose visible. This indirect accumulation is preferable to announcing a transformation with a tabulation of reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat inner thought as dramatic action
rubrics_metrics.description: Transform the picture of a mind into an enacted play so that the advantages of drama (suddenness, relief, immediacy) are available even for undramatic subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use theatrical metaphors and staging: let inner images 'crowd across the stage' and choreograph the play of thought so a crisis can strike with the force of dramatic action (e.g., Strether’s outburst in the garden).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulate POV distance: keep POV but allow apparent objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: While preserving a single character’s point of view, the author can sometimes keep that character’s consciousness out of sight during a scene so the character appears as an objective figure for the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame scenes 'in' a character’s experience but refrain from exploring his thought at moments when his speech and comportment make him seem an independent person; this sleight of hand creates dramatic detachment without abandoning POV.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary or forced dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not effective to 'pepper the surface with animated dialogue' when characters have nothing to contribute; such talk cheapens and discredits their speech when it is truly required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure dialogue is motivated and serves the dramatization. Do not insert talk merely to simulate drama—dialogue should be used fundamentally to animate the actual elements of the picture, not to fill space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scenes to supply past facts instead of lump narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-crafted scene can put the reader in possession of past facts that otherwise would be handled by a lump of narration or 'harking back to make up.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where necessary background facts must be given, try to have them emerge naturally through scenes and conversation (as James’s opening conversation does) rather than through summary exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reveal crucial facts implicitly through small signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical knowledge (e.g., Milly’s love and illness) can be communicated by small, seemingly insignificant words, looks, or glimpses which later 'spring up complete and solid' in the reader’s attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surround the fact and detach it by implication: give brief, emblematic glimpses spread through the text so the reader pieces together the truth, rather than walking straight to the fact and stating it outright. This builds solidity and weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply a 'stereoscopic' view—show periphery from multiple angles
rubrics_metrics.description: Enable the onlooker to see around the object—left and right—so that the impression acquires depth and solidity, much as two eyes shape a sphere stereoscopically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Devote attention to peripheral, non-central moments and surfaces of consciousness; by rounding the subject with varied outer glimpses the central fact is made to register with greater dimensionality than a direct account could produce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the narrator only when he adds value; prefer direct dramatization otherwise
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless the presence of a 'seer and a recorder' contributes positively to the effect, the narrator is dispensable and a direct view is preferable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the narrator performs an economy or adds an effect the story needs. If a narrator’s vantage enriches theme or aids comprehension, keep him; if not, assign point of view directly to the scenes and the reader’s observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Layer methods—'method upon method' and experiment with modulations
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel's language can be extended by combining and modulating techniques (vision-of-a-vision, dramatization of thought, etc.), opening rich possibilities for future practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be conscious of the faculties you employ and those you refuse; mix techniques deliberately to achieve novel effects. Critics and practitioners should analyze and assimilate these combinations rather than attributing them solely to an author's idiosyncrasy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid first-person narrator when it would undermine dramatic suspense
rubrics_metrics.description: In some stories (e.g., murder mysteries) certain persons cannot serve as reliable narrators because admitting us into their mind would betray secrets the plot requires the reader to guess.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a narrator whose knowledge and reticence fit the story’s needs. A murderer as narrator typically cannot withhold the interior information that suspense or puzzle plots depend upon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare and undercut flat impressions by careful approach to turns of events
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'undercutting' of a flat impression happens when a turn of events is carefully prepared and deliberately approached so that it emerges as drama rather than as mere statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure lead-up and handling of key moments so that revelations or reversals feel enacted and earned. Deliberate staging and the patient accumulation of signs allow a dramatic turn to feel both inevitable and surprising.
